edges.effect_quant: Across 2025 meta-analyses of randomized bile-acid-diarrhea trials, sequestrants significantly improved stool frequency and consistency, which is the clinical expression of slower, better-controlled colonic transit in bile-acid-driven diarrhea. A dedicated 2010 randomized physiology study also showed that colesevelam delayed ascending-colon emptying by roughly 4 hours in IBS-D patients, although its overall whole-colon transit effect was modest.
edges.population: adults with bile acid diarrhea or diarrhea-predominant IBS treated with bile acid sequestrants such as colesevelam
edges.mechanism: Bile acid sequestrants alter gut motility indirectly by binding intraluminal bile acids that would otherwise accelerate colonic secretion and transit. Their clinical effect is therefore context-dependent: they can normalize excessively fast bowel motility in bile-acid diarrhea, but they do not uniformly improve every motility phenotype and can overshoot toward cramping or constipation.
edges.summary: Bile acid sequestrants change gut motility in a useful way when excess bile acids are driving fast, loose stools, but the effect is not a simple universal motility enhancer. Randomized trials and recent meta-analyses show that these drugs can slow transit enough to improve stool consistency and frequency in bile-acid diarrhea, while physiology studies suggest the transit effect is modest and phenotype-dependent.
edges.caveats: This edge is about bile-acid-related rapid transit, not about motility disorders in general. Benefits are strongest when bile-acid diarrhea is objectively present, and the same slowing effect can become a downside in people without that mechanism or in those prone to constipation and abdominal cramping.
